mark: Census/ACS, surveillance, commuting, weather, geography, generic upload
note: Verified against the installed 2.0.0b1 release rather than asserted: 42 ADRIOs across nine modules of epymorph.adrio, every one parameterised by the geographic scope and date range the user asks for, and cached. acs5 (9): Population, PopulationByAge, PopulationByAgeTable, PopulationByRace, MedianAge, MedianIncome, AverageHouseholdSize, GiniIndex, DissimilarityIndex. cdc (12): COVID county cases, COVID and influenza facility- and state-level hospitalization, daily influenza state hospitalization, current state admissions and ICU occupancy, county and state deaths, COVID vaccination. commuting_flows (1) and lodes (4): Commuters, plus CommutersByAge, CommutersByEarnings, CommutersByIndustry. prism (4): Temperature, Precipitation, DewPoint, VaporPressureDeficit; humidity (2): AbsoluteHumidity, RelativeHumidity, derived. us_tiger (5): GeometricCentroid, InternalPoint, LandAreaM2, Name, PostalCode. csv (4) and numpy (1): CSVFileN, CSVFileTxN, CSVFileNxN, CSVFileAxN, NumpyFile, the generic ingest for data with no ADRIO. Scope is stated as US because every live source is a US one (Census ACS5, Census Commuting Flows, LEHD LODES, CDC via SODA, PRISM, TIGER); that is the honest counterpoint to Epydemix, which is worldwide but covers only demography and contact matrices. The distinguishing claim is breadth of data *type* (surveillance, movement and weather, none of which any other package in the table retrieves), not geographic reach.
source: epymorph 2.0.0b1 installed; epymorph.adrio.{acs5,cdc,commuting_flows,lodes,prism,humidity,us_tiger,csv,numpy} class inventory

note: epymorph has no built-in forecast scoring. epymorph.forecasting supplies the generation half properly -- a ForecastSimulator that continues a fitted EnKF or particle filter past its available observations, plus munge_pipeline_output and plotting -- but the package contains no scoring rules (verified by inspection of 2.0.0b1: no WIS, CRPS, log score or interval coverage anywhere). WIS, interval coverage and median absolute error are supplied by this manuscript's own demolib.scoring, which ships with the demos, not by the package (JM confirmed, 2026-09-21). Recording this as No is what makes the row worth having: only surveillance/hhh4 and pypfilt/epifx score forecasts in-package.
source: epymorph 2.0.0b1 installed: epymorph/forecasting/ inspected; demolib/scoring.py

note: Hard call because the capability is split across the project. The gempyor package itself has no data layer: subpop_setup requires a user-supplied geodata.csv (columns subpop, population) and mobility.csv (columns ori, dest, amount), and the docs' examples are toy two-province populations. The flepiMoP repository, however, ships a datasetup/ layer that does real acquisition: usdata/us_county_census_2019.parquet and usdata/united-states-commutes/commute_data.gz.parquet (US county populations and commuting flows), population/GLOBAL_age_pop_{1yr,5yr}.parquet (global age structure), build_US_setup.R to turn them into geodata/mobility, build_covid_data.R to pull ground truth from the Delphi Epidata/covidcast API, and build_flu_data.R to pull CDC FluSight truth data. This is a correction: both tables currently mark FlepiMoP as having no automated surveillance-data acquisition at all.
source: flepiMoP gitbook (gempyor > model-implementation > specifying population structure); HopkinsIDD/flepiMoP repo, datasetup/

note: CHANGED from No to Yes: the current mark is contradicted by the documentation. FlepiMoP specifies the compartmental model declaratively in the configuration file -- a 'compartments' section listing the states and a 'seir: transitions' section giving source, destination, proportional_to, rate and proportion_exponent for each transition. The docs describe it as a deliberate design choice: 'We originally considered asking users to specify each compartment and transition manually. However, we quickly found that this created long, confusing configuration files, and so we created a shorthand to more succinctly specify both compartments and transitions between them. This works especially well for models where individuals are stratified by other properties (like age, vaccination status, etc.)'. No diagram generation or data-requirement analysis, so it is the same shape of capability as odin's and SimInf's.
source: flepiMoP gitbook, gempyor > model-implementation > specifying compartmental model

note: No scoring in the package. postprocessing/ holds plotting, run diagnostics and hub submission formatting (run_sim_processing_FluSightExample.R); forecasts are scored by the hub that receives them, externally. Marked No for the same reason as epymorph.
source: HopkinsIDD/flepiMoP repo, postprocessing/ listing

capability: Forecast generation from a fitted model
note: Changed from Mixed to No. The preprint describes calibration in sequential phases with checkpointing as new weeks of data arrive, and mentions scenario projections, but the package's subject is calibration by Bayesian optimisation; there is no forecast generation-and-scoring facility. Forecasting appears as motivation ('epidemiological models reach further by forecasting likely futures'), not as a feature.
source: Fadikar et al. 2025, medRxiv 2025.05.05.25327021 (full text)

capability: Forecast generation from a fitted model
note: Changed from Mixed to No. The preprint mentions scenario projections and calibrates in sequential phases with checkpointing as new weeks arrive, but describes no dedicated facility for generating forecasts from the calibrated model; forecasting appears as motivation rather than as a feature.
source: Fadikar et al. 2025, medRxiv 2025.05.05.25327021 (full text)

note: Ships real data, but as fixed example objects for one historical system, so it fails the reusable-model-inputs rule: measles_cases (biweekly counts, 6 English cities, ~15 years, Dalziel et al. 2016) and measles_covar (census population and lagged birth rate per city); the he10() example carries the same shape. The 6x6 movement matrix in the tutorial is written out as literal numbers in a Csnippet. No retrieval mechanism and no data for any other place or time.
source: Asfaw et al. 2024, arXiv 2101.01157, ss2.2 and 6.2

note: The thinnest mark in this row, and the only thing separating spatPomp from pomp (which is No). The class separates a spatial unit index from the within-unit state vector, so strata could occupy the latter, but there is no stratification construct and the tutorial never demonstrates age or risk strata -- its within-unit dimension holds S, E, I, R for a city.
source: Asfaw et al. 2024, arXiv 2101.01157, ss2.4-2.5 and 6

capability: Forecast generation from a fitted model
note: Changed from Mixed to No. The package is 'an environment for implementing SpatPOMP models, analyzing data using existing methods, and developing new inference approaches'; the tutorial covers filtering and parameter estimation only. Forecasts would be produced by simulating forward by hand, and there is no scoring.
source: Asfaw et al. 2024, arXiv 2101.01157 (full text)

note: Example datasets only, loaded with pompExample() (gompertz, ricker, and the cholera and influenza examples); the paper states pomp has no data automation.
source: King, Nguyen & Ionides 2016, JSS 69(12)

note: Corrected from partial to full on re-verification (Jul 2026), and the evidence is the package rather than the paper: King et al. 2016 mentions ensemble Kalman filtering only in passing as related work, but pomp exports enkf() and eakf() as documented S4 methods (exportMethods(enkf), exportMethods(eakf) in the NAMESPACE, v6.4.0). So pomp offers a particle filter and an ensemble Kalman filter behind one interface, for a single population. Recorded here because the working note this was decided in (knowledge-base/filtering-software-review-Jul2026.md) is not migrating.
source: pomp NAMESPACE v6.4.0 (kingaa/pomp); King, Nguyen & Ionides 2016 for the rest of the row

capability: Forecast generation from a fitted model
note: Changed from Mixed to No, and the paper's vocabulary is a trap worth recording: pomp's 'nonlinear forecasting' (nlf) is a parameter-estimation criterion built from one- and two-step prediction errors, not a forecasting facility -- the paper even argues two-step prediction 'should be viewed as a diagnostic tool'. Forecasts come from calling simulate() forward; there is no scoring and no forecast workflow.
source: King, Nguyen & Ionides 2016, JSS 69(12), s3.6

note: odin is a genuine DSL -- 'R-like code in the odin domain-specific language (DSL) is automatically transpiled into C++' -- so on the plain reading of the row this is a Yes. It is starred because the row as labelled in Table 1 also requires the derived features ('auto diagrams, requirement analysis'), and odin generates neither model diagrams nor a statement of the model's data requirements. This is the row's definition problem, not a fact about odin; see the row-split proposal.
source: FitzJohn et al. 2021, Wellcome Open Res 5, 288, 'odin - A DSL for R programmers'

note: odin is a general state-space DSL, not an epidemiological package: SIR-type models appear as worked examples in the paper's Use Cases and in package vignettes, and the actual epidemiological model (SIRCOVID) is a separate package, mrc-ide/sircovid. So there are ready-made models to copy, but no model library to call.
source: FitzJohn et al. 2021, Wellcome Open Res 5, 288, Use Cases

note: The strongest mark in this row. The DSL supplies array dimensions with implicit index looping and partial sums, 'for example to represent age or transmission classes and the interaction between these without requiring explicitly written loops', and 'An example of adding age structure is shown in the Use Cases'. Still a language feature: there is no operator that stratifies a model you already have.
source: FitzJohn et al. 2021, Wellcome Open Res 5, 288, odin section and Use Cases

note: Same array mechanism as the strata row: regions become another DSL dimension, which is 'used extensively in the SIRCOVID package' (authors' response to peer review), and the paper mentions applying a 'model to different regions'. No metapopulation construct and no movement or commuting model in the package.
source: FitzJohn et al. 2021, Wellcome Open Res 5, 288 (text and authors' responses)

capability: Multiple inference families behind one interface
note: Four methods, one family. mcstate provides a particle filter, pMCMC, SMC^2 and (added in version 2) the IF2 iterated-filtering algorithm -- all built on the particle filter, all behind one interface. Nothing outside sequential Monte Carlo: no ensemble Kalman filter, no ABC, no variational family.
source: FitzJohn et al. 2021, Wellcome Open Res 5, 288, mcstate section and revision notes

capability: Forecast generation from a fitted model
note: Forecasting is a documented step but the loop does not close. Step 8 of the paper's own 8-step workflow is 'Forecast trajectories. If a forecast is required, run the predict() function in mcstate after the pMCMC', and the package handles the RNG bookkeeping to continue particles past the end of the data. No forecast scoring and no rolling-origin evaluation.
source: FitzJohn et al. 2021, Wellcome Open Res 5, 288, workflow steps 1-8

note: Same situation as odin: LibBi is 'a domain-specific language for model specification, then optimizes, generates, compiles' code from it, with declared dimensions and indexed equations. A DSL, but no diagram generation and no data-requirement analysis.
source: Murray 2015, JSS 67(10), abstract and Fig 5

note: Same mechanism as odin, weaker evidence: the DSL declares dimensions (e.g. 'dim n(size = 8, boundary = cyclic)') and indexes equations over them, so strata can be an array dimension. No epidemiological strata construct, and the paper's examples are a physiological model and Lorenz '96 rather than anything age-structured.
source: Murray 2015, JSS 67(10), Fig 5 and s3

capability: Multiple inference families behind one interface
note: Two families on paper, one in practice for epidemic models. LibBi offers the particle filter, pMCMC and SMC^2 alongside an exact Kalman filter, selected by the same command-line interface -- but the Kalman filter applies only to linear-Gaussian models, and the paper is explicit that approximate Kalman-type filters, ensemble included, 'are not treated'. For a nonlinear epidemic model every available method is particle-filter based.

capability: Forecast generation from a fitted model
note: Prediction is a first-class target rather than a pipeline: a prediction is run as its own configuration ('libbi sample @prediction.conf'), taking the posterior sample as an input file, and the paper validates a forward prediction against held-out observations by eye. No scoring rules, and combining inference with forecasting means chaining configuration files.
source: Murray 2015, JSS 67(10), s5.3 and Figs 9, 11-12

note: Example data is synthetic: 'Let us use a synthetic dataset of 1600 farms located within a 50 square kilometer region' -- data('nodes'), u0_SISe(), events_SISe() (four years of scheduled births, deaths and movements). Real movement data is the package's motivating use case but the user supplies it.
source: Widgren et al. 2019, JSS 91(12), s4.2

note: mparse() takes a character vector of transitions in the form 'X -> propensity -> Y' and generates the C code for all state transitions -- symbolic in the sense that the transitions are declared, not hand-coded. Nothing further is derived from that form: no diagrams, no data-requirement analysis.
source: Widgren et al. 2019, JSS 91(12), s5

note: Strata exist only as fixed templates: SISe3 and SISe3_sp hard-code three age categories with their own upsilon_1..3, gamma_1..3 parameters. There is no operator to stratify an arbitrary model, and an mparse() model has no strata construct at all. The 2019 paper does not mention SISe3; the templates are exported in SimInf 11.1.
source: SimInf NAMESPACE and man/SISe3.Rd (v11.1.0.9000); absent from the primary reference

note: Corrected from absent to present on re-verification (Jul 2026). SimInf exports a bootstrap pfilter() and a particle-MCMC pmcmc(); neither appears in the 2019 paper, which covers simulation only. Same evidence as the multiple-inference-families row.
source: SimInf NAMESPACE v11.1.0.9000: export(pfilter), export(pmcmc)

capability: Multiple inference families behind one interface
note: CHANGED from Mixed to Yes. SimInf exports three genuinely distinct calibration families -- abc() (ABC-SMC), pfilter() (bootstrap particle filter) and pmcmc() (particle MCMC), with continue_abc()/continue_pmcmc() -- all taking a SimInf_model. Worth recording that none of this is in the primary reference: the 2019 JSS paper contains no parameter estimation, calibration or Bayesian inference of any kind, so this mark rests entirely on the current package.
source: SimInf NAMESPACE (v11.1.0.9000): export(abc), export(pfilter), export(pmcmc); absent from Widgren et al. 2019

note: Counts under the reusable-model-inputs rule: 'The class pyross.contactMatrix provides an interface to retrieve the individual contact matrices C^H, C^W, C^S, C^O, for several countries' (from Prem et al.), called as e.g. pyross.contactMatrix.UK(); the report also shows age/gender population pyramids for the UK, Italy and India. Bundled rather than fetched, and limited to the countries supplied. No surveillance, commuting or mobility data. This is a change from the current mark of no data support.
source: Adhikari et al. 2020, arXiv 2005.09625, s3.6.1 and Fig 2.2.1

note: Corrected from partial to absent on re-verification (Jul 2026), and it is the one mark in the table that a vocabulary match would get wrong. PyRoss's only sequential Monte Carlo is pyross.evidence.evidence_smc, a density-tempered SMC sampler over parameter space for computing model evidence, not a sequential filter over latent states; latent states go through a Gaussian system-size-expansion approximation. The 'SMC^2' of the PyRoss documentation is not the state-space SMC^2 of Chopin et al.
source: Adhikari et al. 2020, arXiv 2005.09625, ss3.3-3.5 (read in full)

capability: Multiple inference families behind one interface
note: Several samplers, one treatment of the latent state. PyRoss offers MAP estimation, MCMC, nested sampling and a density-tempered SMC sampler for model evidence (pyross.evidence.evidence_smc), which is more than one family by any ordinary reading. Starred because all of them work over parameter space with latent states handled by the same Gaussian system-size-expansion approximation, so the choice does not extend to how the state is inferred -- and none is a sequential filter.
source: Adhikari et al. 2020, arXiv 2005.09625, ss3.3-3.5

capability: Forecast generation from a fitted model
note: Forecasting is a stated purpose of the library and is well developed: a dedicated Prediction section with posterior predictive distributions, 'fully Bayesian forecasts' from models fitted to data up to the present, and Bayesian forecasts of the effect of specific NPIs through their effect on the contact matrix. Starred because there is no forecast evaluation -- no scoring rules, no rolling-origin assessment -- and no operational workflow around it.

Bundled example data is substantive but fixed and single-region: measlesWeserEms (an 'sts' object with weekly counts for 17 districts, population fractions, a neighbourhood order matrix and a map), plus fluBYBW, imdepi and hagelloch. The paper names SurvStat@RKI (https://survstat.rki.de/) as where such data can be queried, but the package does not query it -- no download function.
source: Meyer, Held & Hoehle 2017, JSS 77(11), s5

note: The package ships fitted-model classes, not compartmental structures. hhh4 is an endemic-epidemic negative-binomial regression for areal counts (mu_it = e_it nu_it + lambda_it Y_i,t-1 + phi_it sum_j w_ji Y_j,t-1); twinstim is a spatio-temporal point process; twinSIR is SIR-type but individual-level. None is a compartmental transmission model you parameterise and simulate in the sense this row means.
source: Meyer, Held & Hoehle 2017, JSS 77(11), ss3-5

note: Age stratification is future work in the primary reference: 'A useful epidemic model should therefore be additionally stratified by age group and take the inherent contact structure into account. How this extension can be incorporated in the spatio-temporal endemic-epidemic modeling framework hhh4 is the focus of current research (Meyer and Held 2017).' That extension shipped as a separate CRAN package, hhh4contacts, which carries the POLYMOD contact data and the Berlin norovirus example. Within surveillance itself, strata can only be encoded by treating region x age combinations as extra units.
source: Meyer, Held & Hoehle 2017, JSS 77(11), s5.3 discussion; hhh4contacts 0.13.4 on CRAN

note: The canonical hard call in this row, and it is deliberate (three-tier criterion, JM decision Jul 2026: hhh4 is tier 3). hhh4 has genuine inter-unit transmission terms and a dedicated coupling API: neighbourhood weight matrices w_ji, a power-law decay w_ji = o_ji^-d in adjacency order with d estimated, and time-varying weight arrays; weights 'may be informed by movement network data' or estimated parametrically. But nothing is transported -- the coupling is a fitted regression weight on neighbours' past counts, with weights normalised so that cases are distributed proportionally.
source: Meyer, Held & Hoehle 2017, JSS 77(11), s5.1

capability: Forecast generation from a fitted model
note: CHANGED from Mixed to Yes under the tightened criterion (generation AND evaluation). The package ships oneStepAhead() for rolling one-step-ahead predictions over a test period, scores() implementing proper scoring rules for count data (Czado, Gneiting & Held 2009), calibrationTest() for formal calibration tests, pit() for PIT histograms, and simulate() for long-term simulation-based forecasts. That is the full forecast-then-score loop, in one package, demonstrated end to end on the measles data.
source: Meyer, Held & Hoehle 2017, JSS 77(11), s5.3 (predictive model assessment)

note: One of only two Yes marks in this row. scores() implements proper scoring rules for count data (Czado, Gneiting & Held 2009), with calibrationTest() for formal calibration tests and pit() for PIT histograms, all demonstrated on a held-out test period.
source: Meyer, Held & Hoehle 2017, JSS 77(11), s5.3

note: The strongest data layer after epymorph's. 'The package is complemented by an external online repository (Epydemix Data), which provides access to population structures and synthetic age-stratified contact matrices for over 400 regions worldwide', fetched via load_epydemix_population(); contact matrices come in three variants (Mistry et al. 2021, Prem et al. 2021, Prem et al. 2017) split by household, workplace, school and community, and population data mostly from UN World Population Prospects. Sub-national coverage for selected regions. No surveillance, commuting or weather acquisition.
source: Gozzi et al. 2025, PLOS Comput Biol 21(11), s2.2

note: Models are assembled imperatively -- add_compartments(), add_parameter(), then add_transition('S','I', params=('beta','I'), kind='mediated') -- and custom transition kinds can be registered with register_transition_kind(). Declarative enough that the transition structure is data rather than code, but there is no symbolic expression language, no diagram generation and no requirement analysis.
source: Gozzi et al. 2025, PLOS Comput Biol 21(11), ss2.1 and 2.3.1

capability: Forecast generation from a fitted model
note: The generation half is complete and the evaluation half is absent. 'Calibrated models can then be used to generate scenario projections, forecasts, or explore the posterior distributions of free parameters', with built-in plotting of inputs and outputs, and the paper's case study projects NPI scenarios for Massachusetts. No forecast scoring.
source: Gozzi et al. 2025, PLOS Comput Biol 21(11), ss2.1 and 4

note: 'the summer package provides a domain-specific syntax for the construction of dynamic models of infectious disease transmission' -- a Python API for flows, force-of-infection multipliers, derived outputs and stratification, compiled via JAX. A construction syntax rather than a symbolic form: nothing is derived from it automatically.
source: Trauer et al. 2024, Infect Dis Model 10(1), 99-109

note: summer2 is explicitly a package 'for the construction of infectious disease models' -- an expressive API rather than a set of ready-made SIR/SEIR objects. Worked models are published as a companion textbook of modelling principles, not shipped as callable templates.
source: Trauer et al. 2024, Infect Dis Model 10(1), 99-109

note: Geography is another stratification rather than a metapopulation: the paper's model 'was further stratified into Western Australia (WA) and the other major jurisdictions of Australia', with mixing between locations via the matrix and a fitted 'time to WA fully mixing with the rest of the country'. Mixing between patches, but no movement or commuting model and nothing transported.
source: Trauer et al. 2024, Infect Dis Model 10(1), 99-109

capability: Multiple inference families behind one interface
note: The families are real but borrowed. estival is 'a wrapper for the calibration and optimisation of summer-based models' that integrates them with PyMC (MCMC/HMC and SMC) and nevergrad (gradient-free optimisation), so one wrapper does expose MCMC, SMC and optimisation. Nothing is implemented in the package itself, and there is no sequential filter.
source: Trauer et al. 2024, Infect Dis Model 10(1), 99-109

capability: Forecast generation from a fitted model
note: Changed from Mixed to No. The paper's pipeline runs 'from input manipulation, model construction, execution and calibration, all the way through to creation of the materials for publication' -- an end-to-end analysis pipeline, but a retrospective inferential one. Forecasting and forecast scoring do not appear.
source: Trauer et al. 2024, Infect Dis Model 10(1), 99-109 (full text)

note: The split between the two packages makes this a hard call, and the cited reference covers only the domain-agnostic half. pypfilt is 'deliberately generic and readily applicable to other domains'; the Getting Started tutorial's model is the Lorenz-63 system. The mechanistic infection models are in the companion package epifx, which the JOSS paper does not describe.
source: Moss 2024, JOSS 9(96), 6276 (full text)

capability: Forecast generation from a fitted model
note: Unchanged, and it is the clearest Yes after epymorph's under the tightened criterion: forecasts are defined declaratively in plain-text configuration files, online estimation avoids recomputation when data are revised, and forecast performance is measured with Continuous Ranked Probability Scores. Generation and evaluation both in the package.
source: Moss 2024, JOSS 9(96), 6276 (full text)

note: Forecast performance is measured with Continuous Ranked Probability Scores, and the paper uses CRPS to quantify the improvement from post-regularisation (76.7% in its example).

Bundles real surveillance data, but as a frozen replication extract: EuropeCovid (daily COVID-19 deaths, 11 European countries, Feb-May 2020, plus binary NPI indicator series), EuropeCovid2 (deaths and cases to 1 July 2020, derived from the WHO COVID-19 explorer as of 5 Jan 2021, plus the five Flaxman et al. mitigation measures), and the serial-interval and infection-to-death distributions ($si, $inf2death). Flu1918 comes from EpiEstim, not epidemia. No retrieval. (Correction to an earlier claim of mine in conversation: these carry NPI indicators, not Google mobility.)
source: Scott et al. 2021, arXiv 2110.12461, ss4 and 6

note: One model family, not a library: infections propagate by a discrete renewal equation, which 'is equivalent to a SEIR model when a particular form for the generation distribution is used'. Mechanistic in that sense, but there is no choice of compartmental structure -- the user specifies transmission, infection and observation models for that single semi-mechanistic form.
source: Scott et al. 2021, arXiv 2110.12461, ss1 and 3

note: The model's 'groups' are the unit of partial pooling -- regions in every worked example -- and the paper notes the same machinery 'can be used for multiple regions or groups jointly'. So strata can be carried by the group index, but there is no demographic stratification construct and no mixing between groups.
source: Scott et al. 2021, arXiv 2110.12461, ss3.2 and 4

capability: Forecast generation from a fitted model
note: Forecasting is central to the paper's motivation -- it opens on the CDC FluSight and COVID-19 Forecast Hub challenges and argues that semi-mechanistic renewal models 'can thus be used for forecasting at different tenures' -- and posterior predictive forecasting is supported directly. Starred because there is no scoring or hub-style evaluation machinery in the package.
source: Scott et al. 2021, arXiv 2110.12461, ss1-2
